- Total spent, hires, active ("$45K total spent, 20 hires, 3 active")
- Average hourly rate paid and total hours ("$32.50 /hr avg hourly rate paid, 1,200 hours")
- Industry and company size, if shown
- Member since date ("Member since Mar 4, 2021")

**Client's recent history**
- Past job titles, ratings, feedback given to and received from freelancers, rates or fixed amounts, durations
- Other open jobs by this client

Derived values:
- Average spend per hire = total spent / hires. If hires is 0 or missing, "not shown".
- Average hourly paid: use the stated "avg hourly rate paid". If not stated, total spent / total hours when both are shown, otherwise "not shown".
- New client = 0 hires and no reviews.
- Joined recently = Member since date falls within 7 days before the posted date.
- Mostly long term = most of the client's recent history entries ran 3 months or longer, or most past hires were ongoing hourly work.

## Step 2. Apply the rules

The FAIL and FLAG rules are listed after these instructions under RULES. Each rule has a code (F1, G4) and may carry a "How to apply" note.
Check every rule against the values from Step 1 and the derived values.

- FAIL: any one FAIL rule fails the job.
- FLAG: does not fail the job, but needs a human look. Check every FLAG rule, also on a FAIL job.
- PASS: clears every FAIL rule and has no FLAG.

Accepted regions: Europe (including the UK), North America, Central and South America, the Caribbean, Australia and New Zealand.

## Reference: services

Core work should be one of these:
AI/ML development (Python, Node.js, Next.js, full stack); SaaS development (AI coding assistants, no code, low code, custom code); AI automation; software development (custom code, AI assisted coding with Replit, Cursor, Claude Code); AI agent development (single and multi agent); business workflow automation with AI; AI voice agents (inbound and outbound); mobile apps (React Native, Flutter); AI integration into existing products; RAG and knowledge base chatbots; chatbots (website, WhatsApp, Messenger, Slack); WhatsApp and messaging automation; CRM development and integration (custom CRMs, HubSpot, Salesforce, GoHighLevel); web apps and websites (web apps, landing pages, admin dashboards); API development and integrations (custom APIs, Stripe, Twilio and similar); MVP development; code rescue and takeover; LLM fine tuning and prompt engineering (including model evaluation); computer vision, OCR, document processing; data scraping and pipelines (ETL). UI/UX design and DevOps only as part of a from scratch build.

## Reference: tech stack

Backend: Python, Node.js, PHP/Laravel, FastAPI, Django, Express.
Frontend: Next.js, React.
Mobile: React Native, Flutter.
AI: OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, Pinecone, pgvector.
Voice: Vapi, Retell, Twilio, Telnyx, Deepgram, ElevenLabs.
Automation: n8n, Make, Zapier, GoHighLevel.
No code and low code: Xano, Supabase, Firebase, Lovable, Bolt.
Databases: PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL.
AI coding tools: Replit, Cursor, Claude Code.
Design and DevOps (from scratch builds only): Figma, AWS, GCP, Vercel, Docker.

## Reference: sample match

Stackup has delivered work in RAG systems, multi agent AI, AI voice receptionists and callers (dental, home services), CRM automation (HubSpot, Salesforce, GoHighLevel), AI chatbots with lead capture, SaaS platforms, and clients in real estate, healthcare, legal, logistics, hospitality, automotive, education, field services and nonprofit. A job matches when at least one such project plausibly proves the same kind of work. If a project library is provided below, match against it instead and name the project.

## Step 3. Report

The report covers these parts. The exact format is fixed by the application below.

**Verdict: PASS / FLAG / FAIL**, then the job title.

**Job:** posted time, job type and budget, length, hours per week, experience level, project type, location rule.

**Client:** country, payment verified, rating and review count, jobs posted, hire rate, total spent, hires, average spend per hire, average hourly paid, member since.

**Competition:** proposals, interviewing, invites sent, unanswered invites, last viewed, Connects cost.

**Fit:** one or two lines on the service match, stack match and which Stackup sample proves it.

**Fails:** each failed rule with the actual value. Only when the verdict is FAIL. If the job is otherwise a strong fit, add one line saying it may be worth an override and why.

**Flags:** each flag with the actual value, for example "Hire rate 32%", "50+ proposals", "Average hourly paid $14". Show flags on FAIL jobs too, so the full picture is visible if the person overrides.

**Notes for the proposal:** screening questions and whether each can be answered honestly, any required opening words or keywords, and any timezone or location rule.

writing_docs.title: Banned phrases
writing_docs.content:
# Banned phrases

Never use these in a cover letter or screening answer:

* "Perfect," as an opener
* "I've already built similar"
* "I worked on [project] around"
* "directly aligns"
* "closely matches"
* "exactly the kind of foundation you're looking for"
* "I'm excited to apply"
* "I understand your requirements"
* "I'll approach your system"
* "I'd be happy to" as the closing line
* Any easy out in the close, such as "if you're interested" or "no pressure"
* Any list of more than three features in one sentence

Openers: the first words are about the client's problem, never "I", "We", "My name", "Hello, I", or a project name. The only fixed openers allowed are the ones a type file sets ("Hi [name], thanks for the invite." for Type 3, "Understood." for Type 7, "For your platform," or "For you," for Type 8) or words the client asks for.

writing_docs.title: Modules added by signals
writing_docs.content:
# Modules added by signals

| Module | Added when | What it adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data handling | Compliance signal present | One sentence on access control, encryption and audit logging, naming their standard (HIPAA, GDPR, SOC 2, PCI) |
| Staged autonomy | AI acts on the client's behalf | AI drafts or recommends first, a person approves, then selected actions are automated once proven |
| Integration first look | Integration risk (EHR, ERP, CRM or legacy system named) | One sentence on confirming what their system exposes before committing |
| Estimate answer | Pricing or timeline requested | See the estimate answer rule below. Also listed under "Needs your eye" |
| Team backup | Who they want is "either" or "team" | One line that the team can add capacity |
| Forwardable summary | Decision maker is a middleman | One plain line summarizing the approach that can be forwarded |
| Volume line | Data and scale stated | One line on handling their stated volume |

Each module is one or two sentences, placed where it reads naturally, never as a separate heading.

## Estimate answer rule

Used by every type when the client asks for a timeline, budget or both.

1. No numbers. Never guess a range to fill the answer.
2. Sound confident, not unsure. Frame it as accuracy for their project.
3. Name the details the post does not cover yet, then offer a short call to define the complete scope, after which we align with their preferred timeline and budget.
4. Two or three sentences maximum.
5. For Type 4, say plainly that a rescue estimate depends on the audit.

Example: "An accurate timeline and budget depend on details the post doesn't cover yet, like contract volume, file formats and who will use the assistant. Let's schedule a short call to define the complete scope, and I'll align the plan with your preferred timeline and budget."

writing_docs.title: Screening answers
writing_docs.content:
# Screening answers

* Written separately from the cover letter, one per question, in the client's order.
* Each opens with a direct answer: yes, no, or the fact asked for.
* Then one or two sentences of proof, only from the project library and the profile record.
* The same rules on numbers and banned phrases apply.
* A question that cannot be answered honestly (years in a language Stackup does not use, a system never built) is flagged under "Needs your eye", never padded.
* Certification questions follow the rule below.
* Pricing or estimate questions use the estimate answer rule in `modules.md`.
* Keep each answer under 80 words unless the question asks for detail.

## Certification questions

Only when the client explicitly asks for a certification: a screening question about certifications, or a certification the post lists as required. Never mention certifications otherwise.

1. **Use only certifications on the sending profile** (Certifications in the profile record). Never choose, suggest or invent a certification the profile does not list, even if it is likely the person holds it.
2. **Pick the listed certification that answers the question best:** the cloud, tool, compliance standard or role the client named. Write it as "Certification name, Issuer, year".
3. **One to two sentences:** the certification, then one line of proof tying it to a library project or to the tool the job names.
4. **No listed certification matches:** do not claim one, and do not answer with a flat negative either. Answer with the strongest true credentials (hands on projects with the named tool, compliance work delivered, platform status) and list it under "Needs your eye" as "No matching certification on this profile."

writing_docs.title: Verification checklist
writing_docs.content:
# Verification checklist

Run every item. Mark pass or fail. Rewrite once on fail, then flag.

## Client instructions

- [ ] Every explicit ask and screening question answered, in order
- [ ] Required words or format used exactly
- [ ] Portfolio links included if asked
- [ ] Pricing or timeline asks handled by the estimate answer rule, no numbers, and flagged

## Accuracy

- [ ] Every tool the client named appears correctly, with no alternative offered
- [ ] Every project is allowed for this profile and uses its link in the set order: landing page or mobile, then system, then case study, then staging (case study and staging flagged)
- [ ] Every project and link matches the job's platform: no mobile store link or mobile only project on a web job, no web only project on a mobile job
- [ ] No email address, phone number, contact page or social handle appears anywhere in the proposal
- [ ] Every claim traces to a stored project fact
- [ ] Any certification named comes with its issuer and is listed under "Needs your eye" for confirmation unless it is already in the profile's Certifications list; no screening answer says the profile lacks certifications
- [ ] Every number traces to a verified result
- [ ] No white label work mentioned

## Writing rules

- [ ] First two lines use a detail from this post and say something useful (after the fixed opener for Types 3, 7 and 8)
- [ ] At least one insight the client did not state
- [ ] No banned phrases and no feature list longer than three items
- [ ] No dashes except in project title lines and link lines; no emojis
- [ ] Length within the type's range
- [ ] Structure follows the chosen type file in order
- [ ] No project claim copied from a type sample; every project fact traces to the library
- [ ] Closes on a one line call to action with no question; Type 8 has exactly two questions before it
- [ ] Signature matches the profile record
- [ ] Profile rules followed (for example no timeline or budget for Hassan unless asked)

writing_docs.title: Writing rules for every type
writing_docs.content:
# Writing rules for every type

The chosen type file overrides these rules wherever they differ.

1. **The first two lines are the whole pitch.** They are all the client sees in the list. Use a detail only this client wrote, and say something useful about it. Types 7 and 8 open with their fixed first words ("Understood." or "For your platform,"); the words right after must still be specific to this client.
2. **One insight the client did not already have.** Restating their requirements back to them is not an insight.
3. **Proof is specific.** Types 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8 include two projects in the project format; the second covers a different part of the job. Types 3 and 6 name projects with link lines instead of descriptions. If no genuine second project exists, use one and list it under "Needs your eye".
4. **Plain sentences.** At most three features in one sentence.
5. **Commit to their stack.** Name the tools they named. Never offer "X or Y" when they already chose X.
6. **Answer every explicit ask.** If something cannot be answered honestly, flag it before submitting.
7. **Close on a one line call to action** as the type file describes. No question in the close. Type 8 asks its two questions before the call to action.
8. **Numbers only from the library.** Never estimate or invent a result.
9. **Length fits the type.**
10. **Sign exactly as the profile record says.** Types 7 and 8 put "Best regards," before the signature.

## House style

* Clear, simple English. Short sentences. Always "I", never "we", unless the profile record says otherwise.
* No dashes, except the dash between project name and project title, and in link lines.
* No emojis, no checkmarks.
* No pricing, estimates or timelines unless the client asks; then apply the estimate answer rule in `modules.md`.
* Never mention white label work, such as MD Driven.
* Project facts come only from the project library. Samples in type files illustrate structure; never copy their project claims.

writing_docs.title: Choosing the proposal type
writing_docs.content:
# Choosing the proposal type

Every type is scored against the signals from `job-signals`. Signal names below are exactly the ones that skill produces.

## The eight types

| Type | Required (all must hold) | Supporting (each adds 1) | Exclude when (any rules it out) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 Structured submission | Explicit asks has 2 or more items | Pricing requested · Portfolio requested · Required words or format present | None |
| 3 Invite | Invite is "invite with name" or "invite without name", and the gate did not fail it as a generic mass invite (F6) | Urgency ready now · Decision maker owner | Explicit asks has 2 or more items |
| 4 Rescue or takeover | Project stage is rescue or takeover, or rebuild or migration | Pain frustrated · previous developer mentioned · Integration risk named | Scope size small task with a single defect |
| 5 Architecture or consulting | Role seniority architect or consultant, or Engagement model discovery first with an assessment, strategy or roadmap deliverable | Compliance present · AI acts on behalf yes · Data and scale stated · Clarity vague | Scope size small task |
| 6 Small fix | Scope size small task | Project stage small fix · Urgency ready now · Fixed budget under $500 | Multiple features requested · Project stage new build |
| 7 Problem first | Job focus operations, and the post describes a current problem (manual work, inefficiency, disconnected tools) | Integration risk named · Named tools or APIs · AI acts on behalf yes · Engagement hourly ongoing | Any exclusion for Type 1 except Job focus |
| 8 Approach first with questions | Job focus product, Project stage new build or extend, and Clarity vague or key decisions left open (scope, integrations, data or users not stated) | Urgency exploring · Product type SaaS or platform · Decision maker owner | Clarity precise · any exclusion for Type 1 except Clarity |
| 1 Standard build | Project stage new build, MVP or extend, and Role seniority builder | Scope size project or platform · Named stack present · Clarity precise | Explicit asks 2 or more · Invite · Project stage rescue · Role architect · Scope small task · Job focus operations with a described problem (Type 7) · Clarity vague (Type 8) |

## How to decide

1. Drop every type whose required signals do not all hold, or that has an exclusion that applies.
2. Among the rest, apply this priority: **2, then 3, then 4, 5 and 6, then 7, 8 and 1.**
3. Within the same priority group, the type with more supporting signals wins. On a tie, prefer 4 over 5 over 6, and 1 over 7 over 8.
4. If nothing qualifies, recommend Type 1 and say no type matched cleanly.

## What to show the person

Show the top two or three qualifying types as a visible table before asking:

| Type | Required signals met | Supporting signals | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

Mark one as recommended. The person picks; their pick always wins.

## Adding a new type

A new type needs a file in `types/` with its structure, rules, "Do not" and samples, plus one row in the table above using only signal names that `job-signals` produces. If a type needs a new signal, add the signal to `job-signals` first.

templates.body_html:
Stackup Proposal Architecture (Final Version)

Rule #1: Opening Line

Always start with “Understood.” If the client specifies a starting word, use that instead. Keep tone human and natural, not AI-like.

Paragraph 1: Problem Statement (20–30 words)

Clearly show understanding of the client’s problem. Reflect system complexity, pain points, and inefficiencies. Imply confidence in delivering the exact solution.

Paragraph 2: Sample Work Mention (20–30 words)

Use “I’ve built…” (not “we”). Mention two relevant projects aligned with the client’s problem to establish credibility quickly.

Paragraph 3: Sample Work #1 (~50 words)

Structure: Project title, link, and conversational explanation starting with “In [Project], I have built…”. Clearly connect your implementation with the client’s requirements.

Paragraph 4: Sample Work #2 (~50 words)

Same structure as Paragraph 3. Maintain clarity, relevance, and direct alignment with the client’s needs.

Paragraph 5: Approach (~50 words)

Explain your technical and execution approach. Include tools, APIs, webhooks, and workflow structure. Keep it concise, execution-focused, and within 45–55 words.

Paragraph 6: CTA (7–10 words)

Short, direct, and action-driven closing line such as “Let’s finalize workflow and start implementation.”

Closing Format

Best regards, [Your Name] [GitHub Link]

Critical Rules

  1. Use human, natural tone. Avoid robotic phrasing.
  2. Always use “I”, never “we”.
  3. Ensure every line aligns with the client’s requirement.
  4. Explicitly show how your sample work matches the client’s needs.
  5. Avoid fluff. Keep everything concise and valuable.

Final Checklist

  1. Starts with “Understood” or client keyword
  2. Problem clearly defined
  3. Relevant sample works included
  4. Clear matching of features to requirements
  5. Approach within ~50 words
  6. Tone is human and direct

templates.body_html:
Stackup Proposal Writing Framework (Locked SOP)

1. Tone & Style (Non-Negotiable)

  1. Write like a human, not AI
  2. Use simple, clear, conversational English
  3. Maintain a storytelling flow
  4. Make it feel like you’re already thinking about their system
  5. Avoid robotic phrases like “I understand your requirements” or “I’ll approach your system”
  6. Use phrases like “I’ll start working on…” and “This is very similar to what I’ve built…”

2. Opening Rule (Very Important)

  1. Always start with “For your platform,” or “For you,”
  2. If the client uses a specific keyword, start with that phrasing

3. Proposal Structure (Strict Format)

Paragraph 1 – Approach (40–50 words)

Start with “For your platform…” and explain how you’ll start working, including tech stack and process like APIs, workflows, and integrations.

Paragraph 2 – Sample Works Mention (15–25 words)

Mention 2 relevant projects naturally in a conversational tone.

Paragraph 3 – First Project (50 words)

Project Name – 7–9 word title, then link on next line, followed by conversational explanation matching client requirements.

Paragraph 4 – Second Project (50 words)

Same as paragraph 3.

Paragraph 5 – Question 1 (12–15 words)

Technical, thought-provoking, easy to answer.

Paragraph 6 – Question 2 (12–15 words)

Deeper thinking, encourages reply.

Paragraph 7 – CTA (7–10 words)

Short and action-driven.

Paragraph 8–10 – Closing

Best regards,
Stackup Solution
https://github.com/stackupsolutions

4. Project Section Rules (Critical)

Each project must include title (7–9 words), link on next line, and conversational explanation.

5. Key Writing Principles

  1. Match client’s features, tools, and industry
  2. Show that you’ve already solved similar problems
  3. Avoid generic claims and buzzwords

6. What Makes This High-Converting

  1. Client feels you’ve already built this
  2. Builds trust and relevance
  3. Questions trigger reply instinct

7. Quick Checklist Before Sending

  1. Starts with “For your platform / For you”
  2. Conversational tone
  3. Projects include title + link + explanation
  4. Questions are engaging
  5. CTA is strong and concise

templates.body_html:
Upwork Proposal Writing System (Final Locked Version)

Core Rule

You are not an AI. You are a human expert who has already solved similar problems. Every proposal should feel conversational, confident, and tailored—never generic.

Proposal Structure

1. Paragraph 1 — Solution + Experience + Metrics (40–45 words)

  1. Start with “Perfect,” (or client’s specified word if mentioned)
  2. Clearly state the solution to their problem
  3. Mention similar project names (at least 2)
  4. Add relevant performance improvement (%) based on client problem
  5. Keep it result-driven, not descriptive

2. Paragraph 2 — Project Reference 1 (40–50 words)

  1. Project Name – 7–8 word descriptive title
  2. Next line: Project link
  3. Start explanation in conversational tone
  4. Explain what you built (features/specs)
  5. Explain how it directly relates to client’s problem

3. Paragraph 3 — Project Reference 2 (40–50 words)

  1. Project Name – 7–8 word descriptive title
  2. Next line: Project link
  3. Start explanation in conversational tone
  4. Explain what you built (features/specs)
  5. Explain how it directly relates to client’s problem

4. Paragraph 4 — Approach (~50 words)

  1. Start conversationally: “For your project, I’ll…” or “For you, I’ll…”
  2. Include approach, light tech stack mention, and architecture thinking
  3. Balance: 50% general explanation, 50% technical clarity
  4. Do NOT mention timeline/budget unless client explicitly asks

5. Paragraph 5 — CTA (9–11 words)

Short, confident, action-oriented. No begging or over-politeness.

6. Closing

Best regards,
Anum Ahmad
GitHub Profile Link

Critical Writing Rules

Do:

  1. Sound like a problem-solver, not applicant
  2. Be specific to client’s workflow
  3. Use real system language (automation, workflows, integrations)
  4. Show you’ve already done this before
  5. Keep tone simple, clear, human

Do Not:

  1. Do not use phrases like “I am excited to apply…”
  2. Do not over-explain technical details
  3. Do not write long, complex sentences
  4. Do not sound like a template or AI
  5. Do not add unnecessary fluff

Positioning Strategy

You are not selling services. You are showing: “I’ve already built this system. I just need to implement it for you.”

Final Mindset

  1. This person understands my system
  2. This person has already built something similar
  3. This person can execute without hand-holding

templates.description: Chosen when: new build, MVP or extend; builder role; no explicit asks. Length: 170 to 240 words.
templates.body_html:
Type 1. Standard Build

Chosen when: new build, MVP or extend; builder role; no explicit asks.

Length: 170 to 240 words.

Structure

  1. Hook, two lines. Natural, pain focused, and specific to this client.
  2. Proof, two projects. Each in the project format below.
  3. Plan. Their stack, committed. The first thing we would build and why. Name the concrete tools, APIs, webhooks and workflow pieces involved, in about 45 to 55 words.
  4. Close. A general call to action in one line. No question.
  5. Signature from the profile record.

Hook rules

  1. Start from the pain, not the project. Ask what is costing the client money, time or customers right now.
  2. Use a detail only this client wrote, so it is clear the post was read.
  3. Line one names the pain. Line two shows what causes it or how to avoid it. The second line earns the click.
  4. Sound like a person talking. If it sounds like a lecture, a slogan or a sales line, rewrite it.
  5. No talk about us in the first two lines. No project names, no stats, no "I can build".

Project format

Every proposal includes two projects. The second covers a different part of the job and is never a padded weak match. If no genuine second project exists, use one and list it under "Needs your eye".

Project Name – Project Title
[project link]

Project description.

Project title rules

  1. Seven to nine words, one line.
  2. Targets the main feature this client needs, their industry, and the tech stack they named.
  3. Written fresh for each job. The same project gets a different title for a different job.
  4. Only true details. The stack in the title must be what the project actually used, from the library.
  5. The dash between project name and title is allowed.

Project description rules. Two or three plain sentences, written as a direct match to the job:

  1. What I built and with what. The features from this project that match the client's required features, and the stack used.
  2. Why it matters to them. Tie it directly to their feature, stack or industry.
  3. Result, if verified. Only from the library, never estimated.

When the industry differs, say why the work carries over. At most three features per sentence.

Close rules

  1. One line, 9 to 11 words.
  2. Invites a clear next step, such as a short call to walk through their build.
  3. Confident and forward looking. No question mark, no easy out, no banned phrases.

Example: "Let's set up a short call to walk through your build."

Estimates

If the client asks for timeline or budget, apply the estimate answer rule in ../modules.md.

Do not

| Weak hook | Why it fails | | --- | --- | | "I can build your CRM with an AI voice agent." | About us, not their pain | | "You need a CRM that integrates Retell and Laravel." | Restates the post, no insight | | "Speed to lead is the most important metric in sales." | Lecture tone, generic | | "Stop losing leads forever with AI!" | Salesy, not believable |

Sample

Structure illustration only. Project facts in samples are not verified; never copy a sample's claims about a project. Take every project fact from the library.

Job: home services company wants a CRM on Laravel and React with a Retell voice agent that calls new leads within minutes.

Leads that wait an hour for a callback have usually booked someone else by then. A voice agent fixes the speed, but if it can't see the last conversation it asks the same questions twice, and the lead walks anyway.

Apex Windows – AI CRM With Voice Agent for Home Services
[project link]

I built the lead pipeline and the AI voice agent for Apex Windows, where every call writes its outcome back to the lead record. That's the same call history your agent needs so it never repeats questions to a returning lead.

DentAI Call – Retell Voice Agent for Appointment Booking and Follow Ups
[project link]

I built DentAI Call on Retell with appointment booking and follow up calls for dental practices. The follow up logic there is exactly what your leads who miss the first call will need.

Since you're on Laravel, React and Retell, I'd start with the lead record and the Retell webhook that writes call outcomes back to it. The dashboard, follow up rules and reporting all read from that record, so building it first keeps everything else simple.

Let's set up a short call to walk through your build.

[Signature from profile record]

templates.body_html:
Type 2. Structured Submission

Chosen when: the client lists what proposals must include. Wins over every other type.

Length: as long as the answers need, no padding. Soft ceiling about 350 words.

Structure

  1. Opening paragraph. Two hook sentences on the client's pain, then one experience sentence naming two or three similar projects.
  2. Link lines. One per project named in the opening.
  3. Answers, numbered in the client's order, using their wording as short headings.
  4. Two detailed projects in the project format.
  5. Gaps. Anything that cannot be answered honestly goes to "Needs your eye", never padded.
  6. Close. One line call to action.
  7. Signature from the profile record.

Opening paragraph

Hook, two sentences

  1. Start from the pain behind their most important requirement, not the project.
  2. Use a detail only this client wrote.
  3. Sentence one names the pain. Sentence two shows what causes it or how to avoid it.
  4. Sound like a person talking.
  5. No talk about us in the hook. No project names, no stats, no "I can build", no "I'd build".
  6. If the client set a required opening, use it exactly, then continue with the experience sentence.

Experience sentence

  1. One sentence, 20 to 30 words, in the same paragraph directly after the hook.
  2. Names the type of system and context that match this job, then names two or three similar projects.
  3. Only true claims. Numbers only from the library or the profile's allowed stats.
  4. Plain and confident, not a brag.

Link lines

Directly below the opening paragraph, one line per named project:

Project Name – [link]

Answers

  1. Numbered in the client's order, using their wording as short headings.
  2. Answer every item in full. Commit to their stack.
  3. Proof belongs inside the answers where it fits naturally.
  4. Timeline, budget or estimate asks: apply the estimate answer rule in ../modules.md.

Detailed projects

  1. Two projects, different from the ones named in the opening. Reuse an opening project only when the library has no other strong match.
  2. If the client asks for past work, both go inside that answer. If not, add a "Relevant work" section after the answers.
  3. Project format, title rules and description rules are the same as Type 1.

Close rules

  1. One line, 9 to 11 words. No question mark, no easy out, no banned phrases.

Chosen when: the existing system is broken, unfinished or being rebuilt.

Opening paragraph

Hook, two sentences

  1. Name the likely cause or biggest risk in their current system, using a detail only this client wrote.
  2. State it calmly. Never blame the previous developer.
  3. Sentence one names the problem. Sentence two explains what is probably causing it.
  4. Sound like a person talking.
  5. No talk about us in the hook. No project names, no stats, no "I can fix".

Experience sentence

  1. One sentence, 20 to 30 words, in the same paragraph directly after the hook.
  2. Names the type of takeover or rescue work, then names the projects detailed below.

  2. Only genuine takeovers, fixes or rebuilds, judged from the project overview and case study summary, not from the "Rescue / takeover" tag alone (that tag is over applied in the library). Never stretch a new build into a rescue. If only one genuine project exists, use one and flag it under "Needs your eye".
  3. Project format and title rules as Type 1; the title targets the main fix or rebuild this client needs.

Project description rules

  1. What I inherited and what I did. The state the project was in, the stack, and what we fixed or rebuilt.
  2. Why it matters to them. Tie it directly to their problem, stack or industry.
  3. Result, if verified. Only from the library.

First look

  1. Two or three sentences, after the projects.

Close rules

Source: "Stackup Proposal Architecture (Final Version)".

Chosen when: the client describes an operational system or workflow problem (inefficiency, manual work, disconnected tools, integration pain) and the job is about how the system will work end to end.

Length: about 230 to 280 words.

Structure

  1. Opening line. "Understood." If the client specifies a starting word, use that instead.
  2. Paragraph 1, problem statement (20 to 30 words). Show clear understanding of the client's problem: the system complexity, pain points and inefficiencies, using details only this client wrote. Imply confidence in delivering the exact solution.
  3. Paragraph 2, sample work mention (20 to 30 words). Start with "I've built", never "we". Name two relevant projects aligned with the client's problem.
  4. Paragraph 3, sample work 1 (about 50 words). Project title, link, then a conversational explanation starting "In [Project], I have built". Connect the implementation directly to the client's requirements.
  5. Paragraph 4, sample work 2 (about 50 words). Same structure as paragraph 3.
  6. Paragraph 5, approach (45 to 55 words). The technical and execution approach: tools, APIs, webhooks and workflow structure. Concise and execution focused.
  7. Paragraph 6, call to action (7 to 10 words). Short, direct and action driven, for example "Let's finalize workflow and start implementation."
  8. Closing. "Best regards," then the signature from the profile record.

Project format

Project Name – Project Title
[project link]

In [Project], I have built ...

Project titles follow the Type 1 title rules (seven to nine words, written fresh, only true details).

Rules

  1. Human, natural tone. No robotic phrasing.
  2. Always "I", never "we".
  3. Every line aligns with the client's requirement.
  4. Show explicitly how the sample work matches the client's needs.
  5. No fluff. Concise and valuable.

Checklist

  • [ ] Starts with "Understood." or the client's keyword
  • [ ] Problem clearly defined in the client's own details
  • [ ] Two relevant sample works included
  • [ ] Features clearly matched to requirements
  • [ ] Approach within 45 to 55 words, naming tools, APIs, webhooks
  • [ ] Tone is human and direct

Estimates

Apply the estimate answer rule in ../modules.md.

Do not

  1. Do not follow "Understood." with "your requirements"; the next words must be about their problem.
  2. Do not use "we" anywhere.

Type 8. Approach First With Questions (Writing Framework)

Source: "Stackup Proposal Writing Framework (Locked SOP)".

Chosen when: the client has a platform or idea to build or extend but the post leaves key decisions open (scope, integrations, data, users), so engaging questions are the best way to start a conversation.

Length: about 230 to 280 words.

Structure

  1. Paragraph 1, approach (40 to 50 words). Start with "For your platform," or "For you,". If the client uses a specific keyword, start with that phrasing. Explain how you'll start working, including tech stack and process such as APIs, workflows and integrations.
  2. Paragraph 2, sample works mention (15 to 25 words). Mention two relevant projects naturally, in a conversational tone.
  3. Paragraph 3, first project (about 50 words). Project name and a 7 to 9 word title, link on the next line, then a conversational explanation matching the client's requirements.
  4. Paragraph 4, second project (about 50 words). Same as paragraph 3.
  5. Paragraph 5, question 1 (12 to 15 words). Technical, thought provoking, easy to answer.
  6. Paragraph 6, question 2 (12 to 15 words). Deeper thinking, encourages a reply.
  7. Paragraph 7, call to action (7 to 10 words). Short and action driven.
  8. Closing. "Best regards," then the signature from the profile record.

Project format

Project Name – Project Title
[project link]

Conversational explanation matching the client's requirements.

Tone and style

  1. Write like a human, not AI. Simple, clear, conversational English.
  2. Keep a storytelling flow. Make it feel like you are already thinking about their system.
  3. Phrases that fit: "I'll start working on..." and "This is very similar to what I've built...".
  4. Avoid robotic phrases such as "I understand your requirements" or "I'll approach your system".

Key principles

  1. Match the client's features, tools and industry.
  2. Show that you've already solved similar problems.
  3. Avoid generic claims and buzzwords.
  4. The questions should trigger the reply instinct: specific to their system, answerable in a line.

Checklist

  • [ ] Starts with "For your platform," or "For you," or the client's keyword
  • [ ] Conversational tone throughout
  • [ ] Each project has title, link and explanation
  • [ ] Two engaging questions, each 12 to 15 words
  • [ ] Call to action strong and concise

Estimates

Apply the estimate answer rule in ../modules.md.

Do not

  1. Do not ask questions the post already answers.
  2. Do not ask yes or no questions; they end the conversation.
  3. Do not ask more than two questions.
